```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (!"package:drmTMB" %in% search()) {
  library(drmTMB)
}
```

This guide shows how to ask whether groups differ in their typical spread, and
whether that spread changes with a group-level predictor. It starts with
synthetic Bernoulli and Poisson data, then uses a Gamma model for positive
responses from related groups. The data-generating values are known. The
Bernoulli and Poisson models estimate a random-intercept standard deviation;
they do not estimate a separate residual `sigma`. The Gamma example separates
its conditional response spread from the scale of its latent group effects.

## The model

For a binary response, the group effect shifts the log odds:

\[
Y_{ig} \mid b_g \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left[
  \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ig} + b_g)
\right], \qquad
b_g \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, s_g^2), \qquad
\log(s_g) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 w_g.
\]

For counts, the same random effect shifts the log expected count:

\[
Y_{ig} \mid b_g \sim \operatorname{Poisson}\!\left[
  \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ig} + b_g)
\right], \qquad
b_g \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, s_g^2), \qquad
\log(s_g) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 w_g.
\]

Here, `x` varies among observations and `w` is constant within each group.
The fixed-effect coefficient for `x` describes a change in the mean predictor.
The coefficient `alpha_1` describes how the spread of group effects changes:
because the log link is used for `s_g`, a one-unit increase in `w` multiplies
the random-intercept SD by `exp(alpha_1)`. It does not multiply the variance by
that amount; the variance ratio is `exp(2 * alpha_1)`.

The R formula keeps those questions separate. For example,
`y ~ x + (1 | group)` models the response predictor, while
`sd(group) ~ w` models the SD of the latent group intercept. The group-level
predictor must have one value per group; a within-group predictor belongs in
the mean formula in this scalar-intercept example. More general random-
regression models can use within-group predictors to define random slopes;
that is a different model structure from the intercept-only examples here.

## Make two small synthetic data sets

The examples use 60 groups with 10 observations per group. The two values of
`w` differ by one unit, so exponentiating its fitted coefficient gives the
high-`w` to low-`w` random-intercept SD ratio.

```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(20261017)
n_group <- 60L
n_per_group <- 10L
group_info <- data.frame(
  group = factor(seq_len(n_group)),
  w = rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), each = n_group / 2)
)
group_index <- rep(seq_len(n_group), each = n_per_group)

bernoulli_data <- group_info[group_index, , drop = FALSE]
bernoulli_data$x <- stats::rnorm(nrow(bernoulli_data))
bernoulli_b <- exp(-0.4 + 0.45 * group_info$w) *
  stats::rnorm(n_group)
bernoulli_data$y <- stats::rbinom(
  nrow(bernoulli_data),
  size = 1,
  prob = stats::plogis(
    -0.25 + 0.5 * bernoulli_data$x + bernoulli_b[group_index]
  )
)

poisson_data <- group_info[group_index, , drop = FALSE]
poisson_data$x <- stats::rnorm(nrow(poisson_data))
poisson_b <- exp(-0.4 + 0.45 * group_info$w) *
  stats::rnorm(n_group)
poisson_data$y <- stats::rpois(
  nrow(poisson_data),
  lambda = exp(-0.2 + 0.3 * poisson_data$x + poisson_b[group_index])
)
```

Each data set has a binary group-level predictor and an observation-level
predictor. The latent effects are generated with an SD that increases with
`w`. The response-specific intercept and slope values differ between the two
examples, so the Bernoulli and Poisson fits are independent illustrations.

## Fit a Bernoulli model

The Bernoulli likelihood has no free residual `sigma`. The fitted random
intercept is on the logit scale, and `sd(group) ~ w` describes its group-level
standard deviation on that same latent scale.

```{r fit-bernoulli}
fit_bernoulli <- drmTMB(
  bf(y ~ x + (1 | group), sd(group) ~ w),
  family = stats::binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = bernoulli_data
)

bernoulli_checks <- check_drm(fit_bernoulli)
data.frame(check = bernoulli_checks$check, status = bernoulli_checks$status)
coef(fit_bernoulli, "sd(group)")
exp(coef(fit_bernoulli, "sd(group)")["w"])
```

The final value is the estimated ratio of random-intercept SDs between the
two `w` groups. It is not a ratio of event probabilities. Compare it with the
known ratio from the data-generating model, `exp(0.45)`, as a check that the
example behaves as intended; a single generated data set need not recover the
truth exactly.

## Fit a Poisson model

In the Poisson model, the latent intercept is on the log-mean scale. The
Poisson sampling distribution already determines the observation-level
variance from its mean; `sd(group)` describes additional variation among
group-specific log means.

```{r fit-poisson}
fit_poisson <- drmTMB(
  bf(y ~ x + (1 | group), sd(group) ~ w),
  family = stats::poisson(link = "log"),
  data = poisson_data
)

poisson_checks <- check_drm(fit_poisson)
data.frame(check = poisson_checks$check, status = poisson_checks$status)
coef(fit_poisson, "sd(group)")
exp(coef(fit_poisson, "sd(group)")["w"])
```

This ratio also targets the change in random-intercept SD between the two
values of `w`. It does not describe a change in Poisson residual dispersion.

The fixed seed gives these particular estimates. The table keeps their
departure from the known ratio visible; it is not a parameter-recovery or
calibration result.

```{r introductory-ratios, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Response = c("Bernoulli", "Poisson"),
  `True high/low SD ratio` = rep(exp(0.45), 2L),
  `Estimated ratio in this draw` = c(
    exp(coef(fit_bernoulli, "sd(group)")[["w"]]),
    exp(coef(fit_poisson, "sd(group)")[["w"]])
  ), check.names = FALSE
), digits = 3)
```

## Predict the group-level standard deviations

With no `newdata`, `predict()` returns one predicted SD for each fitted group.
`type = "link"` returns the log SD; `type = "response"` returns the SD after
exponentiation. These are model-implied group-level scales, not the fitted
conditional random intercepts themselves.

```{r predict-group-scales}
bernoulli_log_sd <- predict(
  fit_bernoulli, dpar = "sd(group)", type = "link"
)
bernoulli_sd <- predict(
  fit_bernoulli, dpar = "sd(group)", type = "response"
)
bernoulli_sd_table <- data.frame(
  group = names(bernoulli_sd),
  log_sd = unname(bernoulli_log_sd),
  sd = unname(bernoulli_sd)
)
bernoulli_sd_table$w <- group_info$w[
  match(bernoulli_sd_table$group, as.character(group_info$group))
]
head(bernoulli_sd_table)

poisson_sd <- predict(fit_poisson, dpar = "sd(group)")
head(data.frame(group = names(poisson_sd), sd = unname(poisson_sd)))
```

The default response-scale predictions are positive SDs. The `w` coefficient
summarises their systematic change; the group-level values also reflect the
observed design matrix and should not be read as one estimate of the realised
random effect in each group.

## Three kinds of spread

For a Gaussian response, residual `sigma` is an observation-level standard
deviation around the conditional mean. A model for `sigma` answers a different
question from a model for the SD of a latent group effect. See the
[location-scale tutorial](location-scale.html) for a Gaussian example that
models residual spread.

For a Gamma response, `sigma` is a conditional coefficient of variation: the
conditional response SD is `mu * sigma`. A random intercept in the log-mean
predictor describes variation among group-specific log means. Its SD is on
the log-mean scale, rather than the original response scale.

## Related groups: multiplier and marginal SD

A supplied matrix `K` lets latent group effects covary. Write

\[
u \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,K), \qquad b=D_su, \qquad
D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_G), \qquad
\log s_g=\alpha_0+\alpha_1z_g.
\]

Then `Cov(b) = D_s K D_s`, and the marginal SD of the group effect is

\[
\operatorname{SD}(b_g)=s_g\sqrt{K_{gg}}.
\]

Here, marginal means averaging over the latent field, rather than conditioning
on its fitted value. The predicted `s_g` is an SD multiplier. It equals the
marginal SD when the corresponding diagonal entry of `K` is one. Keep the
supplied matrix scale visible when interpreting predictions.

A one-unit increase in `z` multiplies `s_g` by `exp(alpha_1)` and its squared
multiplier by `exp(2 * alpha_1)`. Comparing groups with different diagonal
entries also puts `sqrt(K_hh / K_ll)` into their marginal SD ratio. Neither
ratio describes a change in the response mean.

## A continuous predictor for related groups

Suppose repeated positive measurements, such as plant growth, come from
related populations. This synthetic Gamma model asks whether the spread of
population effects changes along a continuous environmental predictor `z`.
The observation-level predictor `x` changes the conditional mean.

\[
Y_{ig}\mid b_g\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(
\text{shape}=1/\sigma^2,\ \text{rate}=1/(\sigma^2\mu_{ig})\right),
\quad \log\mu_{ig}=0.4+0.3x_{ig}+b_g,
\quad \log s_g=\log(0.55)+0.4z_g.
\]

The matrix has a non-unit diagonal. Its row names identify groups, while the
observations are shuffled so that matrix order and observation order differ.

```{r gamma-related-data}
set.seed(20261104)
G <- 40L
ids <- paste0("g", seq_len(G))
z <- setNames(seq(-1, 1, length.out = G), ids)
k_scale <- setNames(seq(0.7, 1.6, length.out = G), ids)
R <- outer(seq_len(G), seq_len(G), function(i, j) 0.35^abs(i - j))
K <- outer(k_scale, k_scale) * R
dimnames(K) <- list(ids, ids)
s <- exp(log(0.55) + 0.4 * z)
b <- setNames(s * as.vector(t(chol(K)) %*% rnorm(G)), ids)
index <- sample(rep(seq_len(G), each = 12L))
gamma_data <- data.frame(
  id = factor(ids[index], levels = ids),
  z = unname(z[index]), x = rnorm(length(index))
)
mu <- exp(0.4 + 0.3 * gamma_data$x + b[as.character(gamma_data$id)])
gamma_data$y <- rgamma(nrow(gamma_data), shape = 4, rate = 4 / mu)
```

Fit maximum likelihood with the native TMB engine's Laplace approximation.
The residual coefficient of variation is constant, while the latent SD
multiplier depends on `z`. This example requests point estimates only.

```{r gamma-related-fit}
gamma_formula <- bf(
  y ~ x + relmat(1 | id, K = K), sigma ~ 1,
  sd(id, level = "relmat") ~ z
)
fit_gamma <- drmTMB(
  gamma_formula, family = stats::Gamma(link = "log"), data = gamma_data,
  engine = "tmb", REML = FALSE, control = drm_control(se = FALSE)
)
gamma_alpha <- coef(fit_gamma, dpar = "sd_relmat(id)")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = "SD multiplier ratio for a one-unit increase in z",
  Truth = exp(0.4), Estimate = exp(gamma_alpha[["z"]])
), digits = 3)
```

The estimate in this draw is much closer to one than the generating ratio,
despite the repeated observations within each group. One successful fit does
not establish parameter recovery across other draws or designs.

The group predictions let us keep the matrix contribution separate:

```{r gamma-related-scales}
gamma_s_hat <- predict(fit_gamma, dpar = "sd_relmat(id)")
gamma_scales <- data.frame(
  id = names(gamma_s_hat),
  z = unname(z[names(gamma_s_hat)]),
  multiplier = unname(gamma_s_hat),
  marginal_sd = unname(gamma_s_hat * sqrt(diag(K)[names(gamma_s_hat)])),
  true_multiplier = unname(s[names(gamma_s_hat)]),
  true_marginal_sd = unname(s[names(gamma_s_hat)] *
                            sqrt(diag(K)[names(gamma_s_hat)]))
)
gamma_scales <- gamma_scales[order(gamma_scales$z), ]
head(gamma_scales)
```

```{r gamma-related-figure, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Latent group-effect scales in one synthetic Gamma data set. Circles mark model-implied values for the 40 fitted groups. Solid blue lines connect fitted values; dashed orange lines show the generating values. The left panel shows the SD multiplier, and the right includes the diagonal of K. Both are on the log-mean scale. No uncertainty bands are shown."}
local({
  old_par <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(graphics::par(old_par))
  limits <- range(gamma_scales[c(
    "multiplier", "marginal_sd", "true_multiplier", "true_marginal_sd"
  )])
  for (quantity in c("multiplier", "marginal_sd")) {
    label <- if (quantity == "multiplier") "SD multiplier" else "Marginal group-effect SD"
    graphics::plot(gamma_scales$z, gamma_scales[[quantity]],
      type = "b", pch = 21, bg = "white", col = "#0072B2", cex = 0.65,
      xlab = "Group predictor z", ylab = "Scale on the log-mean predictor",
      main = label, ylim = limits
    )
    graphics::lines(gamma_scales$z, gamma_scales[[paste0("true_", quantity)]],
      col = "#D55E00", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
    graphics::legend("topleft", legend = c("Fitted", "Generating"),
      col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
  }
})
```

The points are predicted group scales, not observed response SDs or realised
random intercepts. The right panel rises partly because this synthetic `K`
has larger diagonal entries at larger `z`. Reading that panel alone would
mix the fitted SD trend with the matrix scale.

## The optional Julia interface and prediction quantities

The matched Gamma call uses the same formula, data and raw matrix. It uses
maximum likelihood with a structured Laplace approximation. It needs a
working [Julia engine setup](julia-engine.html); this optional chunk is not
run when building the article. Structured Julia fits currently require the
default `control`, so the native `se = FALSE` setting is not copied across.

```{r gamma-julia-optional, eval = FALSE}
fit_gamma_julia <- drmTMB(
  gamma_formula, family = stats::Gamma(link = "log"), data = gamma_data,
  engine = "julia", REML = FALSE
)
coef(fit_gamma_julia, dpar = "sd_relmat(id)")
predict(fit_gamma_julia, dpar = "sd_relmat(id)")
```

The native and Julia Gamma fits have been checked against an independent
Laplace objective on this data set. That comparison concerns this model and
these point estimates. For ordinary Bernoulli and Poisson random intercepts,
the Julia SD routes instead use adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature. A shared
maximum-likelihood target does not make different integration approximations
identical, so do not assume that all engine coefficients or log likelihoods
will match.

In the R bridge, stored-row mean predictions on this Gamma route include the
fitted group effects. Supplying `newdata` requests the fixed-effect prediction
with random effects set to zero, including when the supplied rows happen to
be the training data.

```{r gamma-julia-predictions, eval = FALSE}
conditional_log_mean <- predict(fit_gamma_julia, dpar = "mu", type = "link")
conditional_mean <- predict(fit_gamma_julia, dpar = "mu")
fixed_effect_mean <- predict(
  fit_gamma_julia, newdata = gamma_data, dpar = "mu"
)
all.equal(conditional_mean, fitted(fit_gamma_julia))
```

| Quantity | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| `sd_relmat(id)` response prediction | The latent SD multiplier `s_g`; multiply by `sqrt(K_gg)` for marginal group-effect SD. |
| Stored R bridge `mu` link prediction | The fixed linear predictor plus the fitted group contribution. |
| Stored R bridge `mu` response prediction | The conditional mean, obtained by applying the inverse link to that predictor. |
| R bridge `mu` prediction with explicit `newdata` | The fixed-effect mean with random effects set to zero. |
| Direct Julia `fitted()` | The direct interface's population-level fitted value, which differs from the R bridge's conditional output. |

Setting random effects to zero does not integrate over their distribution.
Under a log link, the average of `exp(eta + b)` generally differs from
`exp(eta)`. State which quantity a prediction plot shows.

## Check the fit before interpreting it

The compact tables above show every check name and status without printing
long diagnostic messages. The complete objects remain available as
`bernoulli_checks` and `poisson_checks`; inspect, for example,
`bernoulli_checks[bernoulli_checks$status %in% c("warning", "error"), ]`
to read full details for warning and error rows. The checks cover optimizer,
gradient, Hessian, standard-error, and random-effect boundary diagnostics
where available. Investigate any warning or error before interpreting the
coefficients. A clean diagnostic table does not establish that the SD
coefficient is well identified in every design, and it does not assess
repeated-sampling interval coverage.

These are likelihood-based fits. `confint()` returns frequentist confidence
intervals; it does not return Bayesian credible intervals. This guide shows
point estimates and group-level predictions only. It makes no calibrated
interval claim for these examples, so do not report nominal confidence
interval coverage as established by running this vignette.

## Scope of these examples

The executed native examples cover Bernoulli and Poisson models with one
ordinary random intercept, and a Gamma model with one related-matrix random
intercept. Each models the latent SD multiplier using a group-constant
predictor. The optional Julia calls concern those same selected source
routes, with their own fitting approximations and output contracts. These
examples do not qualify other distributions, random slopes, crossed effects,
missing responses or every structured provider.

Native Bernoulli/binomial also has an explicit selector form when a scalar
intercept must be named:

```r
bf(
  y ~ x + (1 | p | group),
  sd(group, dpar = "mu", coef = "(Intercept)", block = "p") ~ w
)
```

That selector names one ordinary mean intercept. For other required models,
check [What can I fit today?](capability-and-limits.html) and
[the formula grammar](formula-grammar.html) before fitting. This guide shows
ML point estimates; it establishes neither calibrated interval coverage nor
a REML result for these examples.
